analysis.one_liner: Raises the fines hospitals pay for refusing to publish their standard prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a Senate vote and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without any cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: A 2019 federal rule requires hospitals to publish a list of their standard prices for services, but enforcement has been weak: the maximum fine is only $300 per day, which large hospitals can treat as a rounding error. This bill would have raised those fines to a tiered schedule — up to $11,000 per day for the biggest hospitals, $20 per bed per day for mid-sized ones, and $600 per day for small ones. It would also have required the Health and Human Services Department to publish a public list naming every noncompliant hospital, and barred hospitals from hiding their price pages from online search engines. The bill died in committee without a single hearing or cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and families, who would be able to see standard hospital prices before getting care and avoid surprise bills, and employers and insurers negotiating with hospitals. People facing emergency care or major procedures — the areas of highest price opacity — would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: It raises the civil monetary penalties for hospitals that fail to publish or update their standard charges, replacing the current $300-per-day cap with tiered penalties that can reach $11,000 per day for the largest hospitals.
It requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to publish a public list, updated every 180 days, naming every hospital that is out of compliance.
It bars hospitals from using webpage coding to block their price lists from appearing in online search results.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals — mainly large hospital systems that do not publish complete, updated price lists — would bear the fines and the cost of publishing prices, plus competitive pressure once prices are visible.

drawbacks.text: Penalties are capped: the largest hospitals could pay at most about $4 million a year, which is small relative to the revenue of a major hospital system and may not outweigh the business advantage of keeping prices hard to compare.

Publishing standard charges does not guarantee patients get those prices; the standard charges may differ from what insurers actually negotiate, so real-world savings depend on patients being able to act on the information.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: patients cannot shop for care or anticipate bills without published prices, and tougher penalties are the main proven way to move hospitals into compliance. The cost to hospitals of posting and updating prices is modest, and the bill includes hearings and a compliance list, so its design is reasonable. Its weakness is that it never advanced, so any benefit stayed hypothetical.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Senate health committee, and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Kennedy introduced the bill on February 16, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action was ever taken: the committee held no markup, the Senate never voted, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over nearly two years.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that have not complied with the price transparency rules are better off: the stronger fines were never enacted, and the current $300-per-day cap remains the maximum exposure. Patients still cannot reliably see hospital prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Noncompliant hospitals; patients still pay blind

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to raise hospital price transparency fines; it was referred to the HELP Committee.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee.

sides.party_line_note: With a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, the bill never drew enough support to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: Hospitals face per-day fines for not publishing prices, public naming of violators, and a ban on hiding price pages from search engines. Compliance costs are modest but the exposure to comparison shopping and enforcement is the point.
